volumes.title: Opening the Books
volumes.text:
For thirty-eight years I, Bartholomew Quill, kept the accounts of the corn exchange in Emberwick. On retiring I was given a clock and a clean ledger, and I found I could not look at the ledger without wanting to enter something in it.

So I am keeping accounts of beetles. The rules are these. One line for each kind found in my garden at Tally Cottage or in the lane beside it. Each to be drawn, measured, and let go unharmed. The target, by the last day of December: one hundred kinds. My sister says there cannot be a hundred kinds of beetle in the world. I believe the true figure is rather higher.

January is a poor month to begin. Even so: seven-spot ladybirds asleep in the window frame, a black ground beetle under the water butt, and something small in the log pile. Balance carried forward: three.

volumes.title: Under Bark and Stone
volumes.text:
February at Tally Cottage, and the beetle ledger stands at three. A beetle in winter does not come to you. You must call on it at home, and its home is under something.

I, Bartholomew Quill, have therefore spent the month lifting things and putting them back exactly as they were, which is only manners. Beneath the loose bark of the old pear: a flat brown beetle thin as a pressed leaf. Under the doorstep slab: a violet ground beetle an inch long, black until it turns, when its edges flash purple like shot silk. In the compost: a rove beetle, slender, with wing-cases so short it seems to be wearing a waistcoat and nothing else.

A beetle, I should note for the record, is an insect whose front wings have hardened into a case that covers the back. That is the whole qualification. Total to date: eight.

volumes.title: The Oil Beetle in the Lane
volumes.text:
March. The beetle ledger I keep at Tally Cottage, Emberwick, now holds fourteen entries, and the newest is the strangest thing I have yet drawn.

I met it crossing the lane on the first warm morning: a fat, blue-black creature as long as my thumb joint, lumbering like a small alderman. Its wing-cases are far too short for its body, as though it had outgrown its coat. When I offered it a twig it leaked a bead of yellow oil from its knees. This is an oil beetle. The books say its young climb into flowers and ride away on the backs of solitary bees, to be reared in their nests as uninvited lodgers.

Also entered this month: two dung beetles, a click beetle that sprang off my palm with a snap, and a ladybird with fourteen spots. I, Bartholomew Quill, counted them twice. Carried forward: fourteen.

volumes.title: The Pond Column
volumes.text:
April, and I have had to rule a new column in the beetle ledger, because a good many beetles turn out to live in water. My pond at Tally Cottage is the size of a tablecloth. It has added nine kinds in a month.

On the surface spin the whirligigs, black beads that circle one another like clerks at a quarter-day. Each has its eyes divided in two, to watch air and water at once. Below them hunts the great diving beetle, olive-brown and edged with gold, an inch and a quarter long. It rows with fringed back legs and comes up tail-first to tuck a bubble of air beneath its wing-cases.

I caught each in a jam jar, drew it through the glass, and tipped it back. My sister has asked that the jam jars be kept separate from now on. Total entered, by Bartholomew Quill: twenty-three.

volumes.title: Cockchafers at the Lamp
volumes.text:
May. Something struck my study window at Tally Cottage last night with a thump like a thrown acorn. Then another. I, Bartholomew Quill, went out in my slippers with the beetle ledger under my arm.

They were cockchafers, which country people call maybugs: chestnut-brown, an inch long, dusted with white as if floured, and flying with all the grace of a dropped parcel. Each carries antennae that open into little fans. I counted the leaves of the fan with a lens. Seven means a male; six, a female. They spend three years underground as fat white grubs and then a few weeks in the air, bumping into lamps.

May is generous. The hawthorn hedge alone gave me a scarlet cardinal beetle, three weevils and a green tortoise beetle that clamps itself flat to a leaf like a limpet. Thirteen kinds entered this month. Carried forward: thirty-six.

volumes.title: The Midsummer Audit
volumes.text:
June, and halfway through the year the beetle ledger of Tally Cottage stands at fifty-four. I passed the halfway mark on the fourteenth, on a hogweed flower, and took a glass of elderflower cordial on the strength of it.

Flowers are where beetles keep their summer. On one flat white head of hogweed I counted: soldier beetles, orange-red, in pairs; a wasp beetle, striped black and yellow and fooling nobody who looks twice, since it has no waist; and the thick-legged flower beetle, bright green, whose male has thighs like a dancer's. On the dog rose sat a rose chafer, a living emerald that hums like a bee when it flies.

All drawn and let go, as the rules demand. My sister, who doubted there were a hundred kinds of beetle in the world, asked to see the rose chafer. I, Bartholomew Quill, recorded this too.

volumes.title: A Light on the Bank
volumes.text:
July. Entry sixty-one in my beetle ledger was made at eleven at night, by the light of the creature itself.

I was walking the lane beside Tally Cottage when I saw a green spark in the grass of the bank, steady, not flickering. I knelt, at some cost to my trousers. It was a glow-worm, and a glow-worm, I can now state with authority, is no worm. She is a beetle: a wingless female, brown and segmented, who climbs a grass stem and lights the last joints of her tail to call down the winged males. The light is quite cold. I held my hand to it.

I read my pocket watch by her at two inches, and drew her by a candle shaded with my hat, so as not to outshine her. Four more kinds from the lime tree complete the month. I, Bartholomew Quill, carry forward sixty-five.

volumes.title: Antlers in the Woodpile
volumes.text:
August, and the beetle ledger at Tally Cottage has its grandest entry. At dusk a stag beetle flew across my garden, upright in the air and droning like a distant threshing machine, and landed on the woodpile.

He is over two inches long, the largest beetle in the country, chestnut and black. The antlers are jaws, grown enormous, and he uses them only to wrestle other males off a log. He could not give my finger more than a firm handshake. His grubs live five years or more in rotting oak, which is the best argument I know for an untidy woodpile.

At the other end of the scale: the acorn weevil, a quarter-inch long, of which nearly half is snout. She drills into green acorns with it. I, Bartholomew Quill, needed the strong lens and three attempts to draw her. Eleven kinds this month. Carried forward: seventy-six.

volumes.title: The Sexton's Visit
volumes.text:
September. A dead shrew lay on my path at Tally Cottage on Monday morning. By Tuesday it had sunk halfway into the ground, and I, Bartholomew Quill, knelt down to see who was responsible.

Two burying beetles, black with bands of bright orange, were digging the soil from beneath it. They are called sexton beetles, and they work as a pair. Once the shrew is underground they will raise their young beside it, and, unusually for insects, both parents stay to feed the grubs, who beg like nestlings. Nature's undertakers are also devoted nurses. I entered that in the remarks column.

Each beetle carried small tawny mites on its back, passengers hitching a ride to the next burial. The mites do not go in the ledger. They have eight legs, and an accountant must keep his categories clean. Eight kinds entered this month, mostly from fallen pears. Carried forward: eighty-four.

volumes.title: An Error in the Books
volumes.text:
October, and I must report an irregularity in the beetle ledger of Tally Cottage. The total reached ninety-one on the tenth. On the twelfth I struck two entries out.

The fault lies with a ladybird. I had entered three kinds from the ivy: one red with black spots, one black with red spots, one chequered buff and brown. A borrowed book informs me that all three are the ten-spot ladybird, a single species that cannot settle on a pattern and seldom has ten spots. One beetle, entered three times.

In thirty-eight years at the corn exchange I, Bartholomew Quill, never let a false figure stand, and I will not begin for the sake of a round hundred. I ruled two red lines and initialled them. My sister says no one would have known. The ladybird would have known. Corrected balance: eighty-nine, with eleven weeks left and the leaves coming down.

volumes.title: Sifting the Leaves
volumes.text:
November. The big handsome beetles have gone from Tally Cottage, and with eighty-nine in the ledger and eleven wanted, I, Bartholomew Quill, have taken up the kitchen sieve.

The method: shake a handful of leaf litter through the sieve over a white tea-tray, then wait. For a minute nothing happens. Then specks begin to walk. Most beetles, it turns out, are tiny, and I have been striding over them all year. There is a pill beetle that tucks in its legs and becomes a seed. There is a round, glossy thing that feeds on moulds, and a brown one with feathery wings, so small that it sat on a comma in the ledger and left room.

Drawing them takes the strong lens and a steady breath. Seven new kinds in a month I had written off. My sister wants her sieve returned. Carried forward: ninety-six.

volumes.title: The Hundredth Entry
volumes.text:
December, the last week, and the beetle ledger of Tally Cottage stood at ninety-nine. A hard frost had shut the garden like a bank on Sunday. I lifted every stone twice. Nothing.

On the thirty-first I gave up and went to the pantry for a biscuit to console myself. In the bottom of the tin, among the crumbs, walked a small brown beetle, oval, a tenth of an inch long, perfectly at home. A biscuit beetle. It had been living in my own house all year while I crawled about the lane.

I drew it, measured it, and, as the rules require, let it go, though I own I carried it to the garden shed first. Then I ruled a double line. One hundred kinds, every one alive and at liberty. My sister and I ate the rest of the biscuits, after an inspection. Books closed. Bartholomew Quill.

volumes.title: The Lamp in Needle Lane
volumes.text:
I am Lettice Brome, seamstress, of Needle Lane in Emberwick, and I sew late. My work-table stands at the window with the lamp upon it, and for thirty winters I have taken the soft tapping at the glass for sleet.

Last night I looked. A small grey-brown moth was walking up the pane on the outside, in January, with frost on the sill. The carrier's wife, who knows such things, says it is the winter moth, and that only the males fly. The female has mere stubs for wings and climbs the apple trunk on foot to meet him.

My goddaughter Posy, who is six and afraid of moths, would not come near the window. So I have made a plan. I shall stitch a coverlet of twelve squares, one moth for each month, exactly as they come to my lamp. This one I shall work in plain grey silk.

volumes.title: The Herald in the Coal Cellar
volumes.text:
February in Needle Lane. No moth came to my lamp all month, and I, Lettice Brome, began to fear my coverlet of twelve moths would have a bare square in its first row.

Then I went down for coal. On the cellar wall hung a moth with its wings folded like a roof. The edges were scalloped, as if cut with pinking shears. It was the colour of a rusted hinge, with two orange patches and a fine white line across each wing. The carrier's wife calls it the herald, and says it sleeps in cellars and sheds from autumn until spring, living on nothing.

So February's moth did not come to my window. I went to it instead. I drew it by candlelight on the back of a bill, and took my coal from the other bin. Its square is rust-brown wool, with two small knots in orange.

volumes.title: A Moth Like a Butterfly
volumes.text:
March. The sallow by the pump in Needle Lane is in yellow catkin, and at dusk it hums with small brown moths come to drink. I have watched them from my sewing window with the lamp turned low.

One came across to the glass on the ninth. I, Lettice Brome, took it for a butterfly at first, for it sat with its wings pressed together above its back, and no other moth I know does so. They were tawny, with ragged edges like a torn leaf. It is called the early thorn. The carrier's wife says there are a dozen thorn moths in the year and this is the first out.

My goddaughter Posy looked at my drawing, though not at the window. She said it was praying. I have stitched it in profile for that reason, in fawn silk, which is harder than it sounds.

volumes.title: Four Eyes at the Glass
volumes.text:
April, and something large struck my window in Needle Lane hard enough to rattle the lamp. I looked up from my hemming straight into four eyes.

It was an emperor moth, as wide across as my palm. She is grey and rose, and on each of her four wings there is a round black eye ringed with yellow, complete even to a white glint, as though it were wet. The carrier's wife says the eyes are there to startle birds. They startled a seamstress. Her kind live on the heath by the marsh, where the caterpillars eat heather.

Posy was with me. She shrieked, hid behind the curtain, and then, since the moth sat still, came out by inches. "It is looking at me," she said. I, Lettice Brome, said it was only looking like looking. This square has taken eleven colours and most of the month.

volumes.title: White Ermine
volumes.text:
May in Needle Lane. The evenings are light now and I light my lamp late, but the moths know the hour, and the fifth square of my coverlet walked onto the glass at ten o'clock.

It was white, with a scatter of black dots, and a furry white cape round its shoulders. The carrier's wife had the name at once: the white ermine, after the spotted fur that trims a judge's robe. When I tapped the pane it did not fly. It curled its body and showed a flash of yellow beneath, which is a warning, she says, that it tastes foul.

It is the easiest moth I have stitched: white silk, black seed-stitches, done in two evenings. My goddaughter Posy counted the dots on the drawing and made it thirty-one. She asked whether the real one had as many. I, Lettice Brome, said she might come and count.

volumes.title: Pink at the Honeysuckle
volumes.text:
June. I did not need the lamp for this one. At dusk the honeysuckle under my window in Needle Lane smells strongest, and that is when the elephant hawk-moth comes to it.

Nobody warned me a moth could be pink. It is rose and olive green, like a sweet from a jar. It is plump and swift, and it does not settle on the flower. It hangs in the air before it with its wings a blur, and unrolls a tongue as long as its body. The elephant in the name is its caterpillar, which has a snout like a trunk.

Posy watched from my lap with the window open, which three months ago she would not have borne. She held quite still. I, Lettice Brome, have used the pink silk I was saving for a christening gown. The coverlet is half done: six squares, none of them dull.

volumes.title: The Tiger and the Woolly Bear
volumes.text:
July, and the warm nights bring so many moths to my lamp in Needle Lane that I sew with the window shut and choose among them. This month there was no choosing. The garden tiger chose itself.

Its front wings are cream, covered with chocolate-brown blotches like the map of some country all islands. Then it lifts them, and beneath are hind wings of bright orange spotted with blue-black. I gasped aloud. The carrier's wife says the colours tell birds to leave it be.

Its caterpillar is the woolly bear, brown and long-haired, which my goddaughter Posy kept in a box all spring and fed on dock leaves without a notion of what it would become. I, Lettice Brome, showed her my drawing. She looked from the box to the paper and back. "Mine will do that?" It spun its cocoon in June. We are both waiting.

volumes.title: An Old Lady Calls
volumes.text:
August in Needle Lane. I found this month's moth behind the parlour curtain when I shook it out: a large dark creature that dropped to the sill and sat there with its wings spread flat.

It is called the old lady. The wings are brown and grey, in fine wavy bands, like the shawl my grandmother wore to chapel. The carrier's wife says it hides in houses and sheds by day, and comes out at night for sweet things. It cares little for lamps but will come to a smear of jam.

So an old lady came to call upon an old lady, and I, Lettice Brome, gave her jam on a saucer. My goddaughter Posy thought this the funniest thing that had ever happened. Her woolly bear has hatched: a garden tiger, orange and cream. She opened the box at my window herself and let it go.

volumes.title: The Crumpled Leaf
volumes.text:
September. I, Lettice Brome, swept a dead leaf off my windowsill in Needle Lane, and the leaf opened its wings and flew back.

It is a moth called the angle shades. At rest it folds its wings lengthwise into creases, so that it looks like a withered leaf, curled at the edges. The colours are olive and pinkish brown, with a darker triangle across the middle. I have sewn pleats all my life and never made one so convincing.

It set me a difficulty. A moth that looks like a leaf, embroidered, looks like an embroidered leaf. I unpicked the square twice. In the end I stitched it sitting upon a leaf of green felt, so the eye can tell them apart. My goddaughter Posy found it in four seconds. She is seven now, and has begun a moth list of her own, in pencil, with eleven names.

volumes.title: The Marvel of the Day
volumes.text:
October. The oak at the end of Needle Lane is turning, and from it, on the first cold night, came the moth I count the most beautiful of my year at this window.

It is green. Not leaf-green, but the pale, silvery green of the lichen on old bark, marbled with black and white. It has a foreign name, merveille du jour, which the carrier's wife tells me means "marvel of the day". It lives on oaks. Set on a lichened branch it would vanish entirely; on my window glass, with the lamp behind, it shone like a brooch.

I, Lettice Brome, had no silk of that colour. I mixed two threads in one needle, sea-green and grey, and the effect is nearly right. Ten squares are done. Posy has laid them out on the floor in their order and announced that the coverlet wants only two more moths.

volumes.title: Feathers in the Fog
volumes.text:
November in Needle Lane, and fog most nights. I, Lettice Brome, sat nine evenings at my sewing window without a moth, and trimmed the lamp so often that I wore out a wick.

On the tenth evening one came out of the murk and clung to the frame. It was the colour of a fox, with two dark lines across each wing. Its antennae were what held me. They were feathered on both sides, like two tiny ferns. The carrier's wife calls it the feathered thorn. The male wears those plumes, she says, to scent a female through a quarter-mile of fog, though he cannot see his own feet.

I worked the feathers in single strands of brown silk. Eleven squares. My goddaughter Posy asks every day whether December has a moth at all. I have told her the truth, which is that I do not know.

volumes.title: The December Moth
volumes.text:
December. The answer came on a mild, wet night a week before midwinter. My goddaughter Posy was staying in Needle Lane, and it was she who saw it first and called me from the stairs.

A moth sat on the glass of my sewing window, stout and furry as a bumblebee in an overcoat. It was charcoal-dark, with a cream line curving across each wing. The carrier's wife says it is named the December moth, and that it never eats: it has no mouth to speak of, and lives its few weeks on what it stored as a caterpillar.

Posy held the lamp steady while I drew. She was not afraid, and has not been for months. I, Lettice Brome, stitched the last square in black wool. The coverlet has twelve moths, one for every month at my window. It is on Posy's bed now. She says they keep watch.

volumes.title: The Winter Cluster
volumes.text:
I am Silas Combe, and I keep bees in the orchard at Hollowbank, a mile out of Emberwick on the Lowland road. This book follows one hive, the blue one under the old pear, through a single year. I begin in January, with snow on its roof.

You would think it empty. Put your ear to the wood, though, and there is a low, steady hum, like a kettle a long way off. Inside, some ten thousand bees hang in a ball upon the combs, with their queen at the centre. They do not sleep. They shiver their wing muscles to make heat, and take turns, the cold ones on the outside working inward.

Their fuel is the honey they stored in summer. The ball creeps slowly across the comb, eating as it goes. My whole task this month is to leave them alone. It is harder than it sounds.

volumes.title: First Flights
volumes.text:
February at Hollowbank orchard. On the first mild noon of the year the bees of the blue hive came out, a few dozen at a time, flew a short loop in the sunshine and went back in.

I, Silas Combe, had been waiting for it. A bee will not foul her own hive. She holds on through weeks of cold, and on the first warm day she must fly. After that there is work: the dead of the winter are carried out and dropped in the grass, tidy as a housemaid shaking a cloth.

By the month's end they were on the snowdrops and crocuses under the wall, coming home with orange pellets of pollen packed on their hind legs. Pollen is food for the young. So I know, without opening the lid, that in the warm middle of the cluster the queen has begun to lay.

volumes.title: Her Majesty
volumes.text:
March. On a warm afternoon I, Silas Combe, lifted the lid of the blue hive at Hollowbank for the first time this year, and went looking for one bee among thousands.

I found her on the fourth comb. The queen is longer than her daughters, with a tapering body and short wings, and she walks slowly while everything around her hurries. A ring of workers faces her always, touching and feeding her. I call her Madam. She is in her third spring.

She is not a ruler. She gives no orders. She is the mother of every bee in the hive, and her life is to lay eggs: one to a cell, a white grain stood on end, many hundreds in a day. Round her the comb was filled in arcs: eggs, then pearly grubs, then cells capped with brown wax. I closed the lid. All is well.

volumes.title: The House Bees
volumes.text:
April, with the plum blossom out at Hollowbank orchard and the blue hive growing by the day. This month I write about the bees a visitor never sees, the young ones who have not yet been outdoors.

A worker bee's life is a ladder of trades. New-hatched, she cleans cells. In a few days she becomes a nurse, feeding the grubs many hundreds of times a day. At about twelve days she can make wax. It comes from her own body in little clear flakes under the belly, which she chews and moulds. With it the builders raise the comb, each cell six-sided and each wall shared with its neighbours, with nothing wasted.

I, Silas Combe, have been a joiner's son and a joiner's customer, and I could not build so true with a rule and square. They do it in the dark, by feel, hanging in chains.

volumes.title: The Dancers
volumes.text:
May, and the apple blossom at Hollowbank orchard is so loud with bees that you hear it from the lane. These are the foragers of the blue hive, the oldest workers, in the last trade of their lives.

A forager flies as far as two miles and visits hundreds of flowers for one load of nectar, which she hands to a house bee at the door. In a whole lifetime she makes about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey. I think of that whenever I am careless with a spoon.

The best of it is the dance. A bee who finds good blossom comes home and runs a pattern on the comb, a short line with a waggle, and her sisters crowd to follow. The line gives the direction and the waggle the distance. I, Silas Combe, have watched it through glass and I still take off my hat.

volumes.title: The Swarm
volumes.text:
June. On a hot morning the blue hive at Hollowbank poured bees out of its door like water from a jug. The air above the orchard went dark and roaring. Then, in a quarter of an hour, the whole cloud settled on a bough of the old pear and hung there in a quiet bunch the size of a ham.

A swarm is how one hive becomes two. The colony had grown too crowded. So the old queen, Madam, left with half the bees to seek a new home, and behind her the workers are rearing new queens in long cells like acorns.

Swarming bees are full of honey and gentle. I, Silas Combe, held a straw basket under the bough and gave it one sharp shake. By evening Madam and her followers were walking up a white sheet into a new hive. I have painted it green.

volumes.title: The Young Queen
volumes.text:
July at Hollowbank. The old queen has gone with her swarm to the green hive, and for three weeks the blue hive under the pear tree has had me walking about at night.

A hive without a laying queen is a hive running down. The first new queen to hatch made a thin, high piping sound which I heard with my ear to the wood. Some days later, on a fine afternoon, she flew out alone to mate on the wing with drones from hives all over the parish. Drones are the male bees: big, loud, large-eyed, stingless, and good for that one thing. A swallow might have taken her. A shower might.

On the twentieth I, Silas Combe, opened the hive and found a comb with eggs in it. She is home, and laying. I sat down on the grass for some time.

volumes.title: Taking the Honey
volumes.text:
August. The lime trees along the Hollowbank lane have finished flowering and the blue hive is heavy. This is the month I take my rent.

The bees store honey in the upper box. They carry in nectar thin as water, fan it with their wings until it thickens, and then seal each full cell with a lid of white wax. On a still evening I, Silas Combe, lifted out the sealed combs with a little smoke to keep everyone calm. The smoke does no harm. It sends the bees to fill themselves with honey, and a full bee is a mild one.

I took twenty-eight pounds and left them the lower box untouched, forty pounds at the least, for that is their winter and not mine to touch. The kitchen at Hollowbank smells of limes and warm wax, and every wasp in the Lowlands has learned my address.

volumes.title: The Guards at the Gate
volumes.text:
September at Hollowbank orchard, and the wasps have found the blue hive. With the flowers failing, every sweet-toothed thing in the parish would like to rob a bee's larder. This month belongs to the guards.

They stand at the entrance on four legs with the front pair raised, and they meet each arrival. A bee of the hive carries the hive's own smell and passes. A stranger is challenged; a wasp is seized by two or three and bundled off the board. I, Silas Combe, have watched one guard tow a wasp twice her size to the edge and drop it over.

My part is small. I narrowed the doorway to the width of two bees, so that a few can hold it against many. The young queen's daughters are doing the guarding now. They have their mother's steadiness, and, I am sorry to say, her temper.

volumes.title: Ivy Honey and Idle Drones
volumes.text:
October. The last feast of the bee year at Hollowbank is the ivy on the orchard wall, whose plain green flowers open when everything else is over. On a sunny noon the whole wall hums, and the blue hive brings home a pale honey that sets hard as candle wax in the comb.

The drones' summer is ended. They cannot gather food, and the hive cannot feed idlers through the winter, so the workers walk them firmly to the door and will not let them back. It looks harsh. It is only housekeeping, and new drones will be raised in spring.

Something better is happening inside. The bees born now are winter bees. A summer worker wears herself out in six weeks. These are plumper, do little flying, and will live six months, long enough to carry the queen through to the crocuses. I, Silas Combe, envy them their timing.

volumes.title: Shutting Up for Winter
volumes.text:
November. I, Silas Combe, have done the last of my work on the blue hive at Hollowbank until spring, and a list will serve.

One: a strip of tin with small holes across the door, to let bees out and keep mice from moving in. A mouse thinks a hive a fine larder. Two: a stone on the roof against the gales. Three: I lifted one side of the hive an inch to judge its weight, and it nearly pulled my arm down, so they have honey enough. Four: I left every crack alone. The bees have sealed them with a brown tree-gum, better than any putty.

Five is a custom. In these parts you tell the bees the news of the household, quietly, at the door. I told them the pear tree cropped well, my daughter is to marry in spring, and the green hive thrives.

volumes.title: A Candle at Midwinter
volumes.text:
December at Hollowbank, the shortest day, and frost on the orchard grass. I went out and put my ear to the blue hive, as I did in January. The same low hum, like a kettle a long way off. They are clustered around their young queen, shivering themselves warm on lime and ivy honey.

So the year is told. One hive became two. A queen left and a queen was made. Many thousands of bees were born in that box since spring and wore out their wings in the orchard, and hardly one of those now humming was alive when I began this book.

From the wax of the August combs I, Silas Combe, have made one candle. It is burning in the kitchen window as I write, and smells of summer. When it is done I shall go to bed. The bees will keep the fire in.

volumes.title: A Hole in the Lawn
volumes.text:
I am Oswin Tench, schoolmaster, retired, of the Old Schoolhouse in Emberwick. This March I dug a pond in my back lawn, nine feet by six and two feet deep in the middle, with one shelving side so that anything falling in may walk out again.

I lined it with clay from the marsh, trodden down in my oldest boots, and let the rain fill it. That took eleven days. It is now a brown rectangle of water with nothing in it whatever. No weed, no snail, not so much as a gnat.

My neighbour Mrs Aldous looked over the wall and said I had made a breeding place for midges and would be sorry. Possibly. But I have put nothing in on purpose. I want to see who comes of their own accord, and in what order, and I shall write them down here for one full year.

volumes.title: First Across the Water
volumes.text:
April. The pond I dug behind the Old Schoolhouse is five weeks old, and on the ninth it received its first visitors. I, Oswin Tench, looked out after breakfast and there were three pond skaters standing on the water.

They had flown in. Few people know that a pond skater has wings, folded flat along its back. It finds new water by the shine.

On the surface it is a marvel. The water has a kind of skin, and the skater stands upon it on four long legs whose feet are covered in fine hairs that will not wet. Each foot makes a dimple and does not break through. It rows with the middle pair, steers with the hind pair, and keeps the short front pair free to seize any fly that falls in. It feels the ripples of a struggling insect as a spider feels its web.

volumes.title: The Rowers Underneath
volumes.text:
May. My new pond behind the Old Schoolhouse has grown a green tinge and its second kind of resident. Pond skaters own the top of the water. The underside now belongs to the backswimmer.

It is a boat-shaped bug half an inch long, and it does everything upside down. It hangs beneath the surface on its back, with two long legs held out like oars, and when a shadow falls it rows downward in quick jerks. Its underside, which faces the sky, is dark. Its back, which faces the deep, is pale. A film of air clings to it, so that it flashes silver as it dives.

I, Oswin Tench, lifted one out in a tea-strainer, and it flipped over and flew away, which neither of us expected. A word of caution for the record: it can prick a finger sharply. I admire it through a jar.

volumes.title: Mrs Aldous Is Proved Right
volumes.text:
June. My neighbour Mrs Aldous warned me in March that a pond would breed gnats, and I, Oswin Tench, must record that she was correct. The pond behind the Old Schoolhouse is full of wrigglers.

They are gnat larvae, a quarter-inch long. Each hangs head-down from the surface by a breathing tube at its tail, like a comma suspended from the ceiling. Tap the bank and they all let go and wriggle to the bottom, then drift up again. Their mothers laid the eggs in floating rafts, each no bigger than a caraway seed.

I told Mrs Aldous over the wall. She was gracious in victory. I have also noted this: the backswimmers eat them all day, the pond skaters take the adults as they hatch, and four whirligig beetles arrived on Thursday and circle like sharks. A pond feeds itself. We shall see who is sorry.

volumes.title: Blue Needles
volumes.text:
July, and the pond behind the Old Schoolhouse is four months old. I planted nothing, but a water forget-me-not has arrived by itself on some bird's foot, and its stems now matter very much.

All this week damselflies have come to them. They are thin as darning needles and brighter than any thread: the males sky-blue ringed with black, the females duller green. They fly weakly, like blown thistledown, and at rest they fold their wings together along the back. They arrive in couples, the male holding the female by the neck with the tip of his tail. So joined, they settle on a stem. She curves her body down and slits the stem below the water-line, placing one egg in each cut.

I, Oswin Tench, counted nine pairs on Tuesday. That is a great many eggs entrusted to a pond that was lawn in February. I feel the responsibility.

volumes.title: The Hawker's Beat
volumes.text:
August. A dragonfly has taken possession of my pond behind the Old Schoolhouse. He is a hawker, four inches across the wings, striped apple-green and blue, and he patrols the nine feet of water like a constable on a very short street.

I, Oswin Tench, have timed him: eleven seconds a circuit. He can hover, dart sideways, and fly backwards. His eyes are so large that they meet on top of his head. He hunts by catching gnats in the basket of his bristly legs, and he rattles when he turns. When I stand at the edge he flies up and inspects me, a foot from my nose, then carries on.

Mrs Aldous has observed over the wall that there are fewer gnats in her garden this month than in any August she remembers. She said it to her washing, but I believe it was intended for me.

volumes.title: Sticks That Walk
volumes.text:
September. The pond behind the Old Schoolhouse has a carpet of dead leaves now, and I, Oswin Tench, spent an hour watching a small twig on the bottom before I was sure that it was walking.

It was a caddis larva. It is a soft grub, and for protection it builds a tube of silk and sticks on whatever lies to hand: bits of leaf, lengths of stem, grains of grit, sometimes an unlucky snail shell. Only its head and six legs poke out of the front. It drags the house along and backs into it at a touch. Each kind keeps to its own style, as builders do.

Next summer it will seal the door, change inside, and swim up to hatch into a mothlike fly with hairy wings. I found seven in all. One has built entirely with forget-me-not seeds and is the best-dressed animal in the garden.

volumes.title: A Beetle from the Sky
volumes.text:
October. Something landed on my greenhouse roof at night with a crack, and in the morning I, Oswin Tench, found a large dark beetle on its back in the gutter. I carried it to the pond behind the Old Schoolhouse, where it had surely been aiming. To a beetle flying by moonlight, glass shines like water.

It is the great diving beetle: an inch and a quarter long, olive-black, trimmed with yellow all round. It swam down at once, rowing both hind legs together. Every few minutes it floats up tail-first and takes a fresh store of air beneath its wing-cases.

The pond is changing guard. The pond skaters, first to come in April, are leaving. I watched two walk ashore across the mud and into the long grass, where they will sleep the winter under moss. The water looks empty again, but I know better now.

volumes.title: What the Net Brought Up
volumes.text:
November. Leaves from the schoolhouse lime have been falling into my pond, and too many will sour the water. So I, Oswin Tench, have been fishing them out with a kitchen sieve tied to a bean pole, and sorting each load in a white pie dish before it goes on the heap.

It is slow. Everything alive must be picked out and returned. But it is how I found them. Among the leaves crawled slim, pale brown creatures half an inch long, with six legs, wide-set eyes and three leaf-shaped tails. Damselfly nymphs. The eggs laid in the forget-me-not stems in July have hatched, and the young are living on the bottom, hunting water fleas.

I counted fourteen in six sievefuls and put back every one. There must be hundreds. They will spend the winter down there. Mrs Aldous asked what I was grinning at. I said, "Tenants."

volumes.title: Under the Ice
volumes.text:
January, a hard frost, and the pond behind the Old Schoolhouse has a lid of ice an inch thick. I, Oswin Tench, have been lying on a sack at the edge, looking through it, to the alarm of the postman.

It is clear as a window. On its underside hang silver bubbles, and among them a backswimmer, upside down as ever, rowing slowly along like a fly on a ceiling. Water is heaviest a little above freezing, so the deepest part of the pond stays just warm enough, and everything alive has gone down there to wait.

One must never smash pond ice; the shock harms what lies below. Instead I stand a pan of hot water on it until it melts a round hole, for air. Mrs Aldous lent me the pan. She asked whether the damselfly nymphs were all right. I said I believed so.

volumes.title: One Year of Water
volumes.text:
March again. A year ago this week I, Oswin Tench, dug a hole in the lawn of the Old Schoolhouse, and it held brown rainwater and nothing else. This morning I sat beside it with my notebook and called the roll.

Pond skaters, who came first and came back on Tuesday, five of them. Backswimmers. Whirligig beetles. Gnats, as foretold. Damselflies, nine pairs, and their nymphs, now nearly an inch long. One hawker dragonfly. Caddis, seven. One great diving beetle, by air. Water fleas beyond counting. Also a forget-me-not, three snails and a frog, none of whom are insects, but one must be civil. I invited none of them. Dig a hole, add rain, and wait: that is the entire method.

Mrs Aldous came round by the gate, not the wall, and brought a marsh marigold in a bucket. She thought it would suit the shallow end. It does.

volumes.title: The First-Born
volumes.text:
May. For fourteen months I, Oswin Tench, have watched creatures arrive at the pond behind the Old Schoolhouse. This morning, for the first time, I watched one leave that had never been anywhere else.

At seven o'clock a damselfly nymph climbed out of the water up a forget-me-not stem, the same plant its egg was laid in last July. It gripped and went still. Then its back split, and something pale and crumpled pulled itself out and hung beside the empty skin. Over an hour the wings unfolded like wet silk drying. The body lengthened. A faint blue came into it.

Mrs Aldous watched with me from the bench, holding her tea and not drinking it. After nine it lifted off, weak as thistledown, and went over the wall into her garden. The empty skin is still on the stem. Underneath it, the pond skaters row on.
